238.fact: Highest station in the system, platform about 87.5 feet above street level, built tall to clear the Gowanus Canal's lift bridge. Was the highest rapid-transit station in the world until 2022.

95.fact: Opened in 1885 -- commonly cited as the oldest station still in continuous operation in the system.

300.fact: The deepest station in the system, about 173 feet below street level. Its 1,000-foot "Tunnel Street" pedestrian passage to Ft. George is arguably the only underground street in NYC.

611.fact: The busiest station in the entire system, with more than 45 million riders a year.

610.fact: The system's second-busiest station, and the eastern end of the original 1904 IRT subway line.

199.fact: One of the least-used stations in the system -- it sits in the middle of the Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge, reachable only by a causeway through the marsh.

58.fact: The system's largest terminal station, serving four lines at the southern tip of Brooklyn.

236.fact: Has a permanently sealed-off express platform behind the wall, a leftover from a never-completed expansion.

622.fact: Successor to the original 1904 IRT City Hall station, an ornate loop terminal closed in 1945 that the 6 train still loops through (without stopping) to turn around today.

159.fact: A 1998 renovation covered the station in mosaics and murals tracing the evolution of life on Earth, from single-celled organisms to a T. rex, tying into the museum overhead.

475.fact: Part of the Second Avenue Subway's first phase, opened January 2017 -- the city's biggest subway expansion in roughly 50 years, first proposed back in the 1920s.

476.fact: Features 12 giant mosaic portraits by artist Chuck Close, part of the new Second Avenue line's unusually heavy investment in public art.

635.fact: The 2009-built South Ferry station flooded with 15 million gallons of salt water during Hurricane Sandy in 2012. Its century-old predecessor loop station, one stop away, was pressed back into emergency service while it was rebuilt.

328.fact: Destroyed on September 11, 2001, this station sat unused for 17 years before reopening in 2018, featuring a mosaic by artist Ann Hamilton quoting the Declaration of Independence.

26.fact: A six-track junction where the Brighton and 4th Avenue lines merge at grade -- widely considered the single biggest bottleneck in the subway system.

616.fact: The busiest subway station outside Manhattan.

196.fact: The only station in the system that exclusively serves trains heading in one direction -- only Manhattan-bound A trains stop here.

471.fact: The deepest point on the 7 train's 2015 extension, at roughly 175 feet down -- its escalators drop 84 feet, the longest run of any escalator in the system.

416.fact: The northernmost station in the entire New York City subway system.

360.fact: The 6 train's Bronx terminus, opened in 1920, sitting at the edge of the city's largest park.

378.fact: The 4 train's Bronx terminus -- one of several Bronx IRT stations built with the same three-track, two-platform layout.

222.fact: About 100 feet deep with a high vaulted ceiling, since the line dips beneath both channels of the East River on either side. Opened in 1989.

606.fact: One underground complex holds three separately-named stations, connecting the 7, E, F, and G trains -- a rare four-line meetup outside Midtown.

501.fact: Southern terminus of the Staten Island Railway, connecting directly to the free Staten Island Ferry.

502.fact: On the Staten Island Railway, only trips beginning or ending at St George or Tompkinsville are charged a fare -- everything in between is free.

A.fact: The longest line in the system at about 31 miles, with four separate termini. Also crosses the longest gap between adjacent stations anywhere in the system -- 3.5 miles over Jamaica Bay between Howard Beach and Broad Channel.

G.fact: The shortest full-length line in the system, about 11.4 miles -- and the only line that never enters Manhattan.

7.fact: Nicknamed the "International Express" for the immigrant neighborhoods it runs through in Queens -- designated a National Millennium Trail in 1999.

1.fact: Part of the system's original line, which opened October 27, 1904 with 28 stations and a nickel fare -- more than 100,000 people rode it on day one.

GS.fact: At 0.8 miles and about a one-minute ride between Times Sq and Grand Central, it's the shortest scheduled transit route in North America.

FS.fact: Brooklyn's 4-stop shuttle has run its current route between Franklin Av and Prospect Park since 1963.

H.fact: Extends north to Rockaway Blvd on summer weekends to help handle beach traffic.

Z.fact: One half of the system's only skip-stop pair -- limited rush-hour Z trains skip stops the J covers, a pattern dating back to 1988.

6.fact: The IRT Lexington Avenue corridor (4/5/6) is the busiest subway line in North America, carrying more daily riders than San Francisco, Chicago, and Boston's entire transit systems combined.

L.fact: Was the pilot line for the system's automated CBTC signaling, running fully automatic since around 2012. A partial 14th St tunnel shutdown for Hurricane Sandy repairs ran 2019-2020, after a planned full closure was scaled back at the last minute.

M.fact: Didn't have a one-seat ride into Manhattan for 34 years, from 1976 until the 2010 Chrystie St Connection rerouted it through 6th Avenue.

N.fact: Runs on the fully elevated Astoria line, opened in 1917 -- over a century old and still one of the system's longest-running elevated structures.

R.fact: Runs local at every stop with no express version -- nicknamed "the Rarely" for its delays even before a 13-month shutdown of the Montague St Tunnel for Hurricane Sandy repairs.

SI.fact: Has zero physical track connection to the rest of the subway -- Staten Island is the only borough not directly linked. A 1920s plan for a tunnel under the Narrows to Brooklyn was never built.
